title: SkewGuard-PoLR: Investigating Dirichlet-Uncertainty Gated Multi-Cluster Expansion for Prefix-Consensus Self-Consistency

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to hedge against incorrect dominant-cluster selection in prefix-consensus self-consistency (PoLR). None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific objective. While several papers discuss Bayesian clustering uncertainty (e.g., [4], [7], [11]), they focus on summarizing posterior uncertainty or inferring the number of clusters, not on mitigating incorrect dominant-cluster selection in self-consistency algorithms. Papers like [17] and [19] address uncertainty in clustering but do not target prefix-consensus self-consistency or dominant-cluster selection.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves placing a Dirichlet posterior over cluster proportions and triggering multi-cluster expansion when the credible set indicates uncertainty about cluster dominance. Papers [4], [7], [11], and [12] discuss Dirichlet process mixture models and posterior distributions for clustering, including uncertainty quantification and credible sets. For example, [11] specifically addresses posterior distributions for the number of clusters in Dirichlet process mixture models, and [7] discusses credible balls for Bayesian cluster analysis. These works cover the use of Dirichlet posteriors and credible sets for uncertainty quantification in clustering, which aligns with the mechanism described in the contribution.

### Evaluation
The evaluation is presented as a principled Bayesian extension of PoLR that expands all clusters within a credible set when dominance is ambiguous. Papers [4], [7], [11], and [12] use Bayesian clustering methods and credible sets for uncertainty quantification, but none explicitly evaluate a mechanism for expanding clusters based on credible set ambiguity in prefix-consensus self-consistency. The evaluation design appears novel, as no prior paper uses this specific validation setup for PoLR or similar algorithms.

### Domain
The domain is test-time scaling/self-consistency for LLM reasoning. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], and [6] extensively cover test-time scaling and self-consistency for LLM reasoning. For example, [1] discusses stabilization in self-consistency algorithms, [2] addresses adaptive test-time compute allocation, and [5] surveys efficient test-time compute strategies for LLM reasoning. These papers establish that the domain is covered.
